title_full: Symphony No. 6 in F major, Op. 68 “Pastoral”

composer.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
composer.nationality_note: Grove opens the article “German composer” (b Bonn, bap. 17 Dec 1770; d Vienna, 26 Mar 1827), and this set follows Grove. The label names the German cultural and linguistic nation, not a state: no German nation-state existed until 1871. Beethoven was born in Bonn, seat of the Electorate of Cologne — an Imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire, styled “of the German Nation” — and lived in Vienna from 1792 until his death. Across the composers in this set Grove's nationalities track the modern state that now holds the birthplace: Bonn and Hamburg give German (Beethoven, Brahms), Salzburg Austrian (Mozart), St Petersburg Russian (Shostakovich). Grove states no editorial rule for this, and does not always assign a nationality at all — Leopold Mozart, born in Augsburg, is simply “Composer, violinist and theorist”.

era_note: Kept Classical deliberately (decided 21 Aug 2026). periods.json buckets by year and the bucket sets the card colour; Romantic begins 1830, so all nine read Classical. The boundary is global, so moving it to split Beethoven would carry Haydn's late symphonies and the whole of Schubert across with him. Grove's three periods (first to c1802, second to c1812, third 1813-27) divide the nine 1-2 | 3-8 | 9, so the scholarly break falls at the Eroica, not at any date in the 1830s. Second period — Romantic in ambition, Classical in method, and programmatic in a way the Romantics took up directly.

place.polity_note: The Austrian Empire was proclaimed 11 August 1804 and the Holy Roman Empire dissolved 6 August 1806, so the sovereign state in 1808 is the Empire. Heiligenstadt was then a village outside Vienna, in the Archduchy of Austria — country_then names that crown land, this names the sovereign state above it.
place.note: Grove dates it 1808 flatly. Wikipedia's 1802–1808 reaches back to early pastoral sketches. The countryside north of Vienna where Beethoven took summer lodgings is the landscape the work describes.

reason.summary: Written alongside the Fifth, and dedicated jointly to Lobkowitz and Rasumovsky.
reason.dedicatee: Prince Franz Joseph von Lobkowitz and Count Rasumovsky
reason.occasion: Companion to the Fifth rather than a commission: the two were finished together and published together, sharing one joint dedication to Lobkowitz and Rasumovsky.
reason.occasion_spoken: no patron, as the companion piece to the Fifth
reason.detail: It shares dedicatees and a premiere with the Fifth, and Grove points out how deliberately unlike its twin it is: 'the great foil to the Fifth Symphony is the Sixth (Pastoral, 1808), though here for once the first movement is made as quiet as possible.' Beethoven's own caution, quoted on Wikipedia, is that the work is 'more the expression of feeling than painting'.

first_performance.notes: The same marathon concert that premiered the Fifth. In that programme the Pastoral was numbered fifth and the C minor symphony sixth — the numbering we use was settled at publication. On the forces: the same Theater an der Wien orchestra as the Fifth, on the same evening. Brown infers the house strength of 6 to 8 first violins and the rest in proportion; no roster of the night survives.

instrumentation.doublings: None. The piccolo is a separate part, playing against both flutes in the storm.
instrumentation.note: 9 wind, 6 brass, timpani and the five string parts. Trumpets enter in the third movement, trombones and timpani only for the storm and finale. Counted from the score's distinct parts, doublings once. Grove's work-list gives composition dates, first performances, publication and dedications but no instrumentation, so the count rests on Wikipedia's instrumentation section alone and is uncorroborated.

listen_for.hook: Five movements, not four — and the last three run without a break.
listen_for.spoken: five movements instead of four, the last three running without a break
listen_for.detail: The storm is a movement in its own right, wedged between the peasants' dance and the shepherds' song of thanks, and the three play continuously.

listen_for.hook: Three birds are named in the score: nightingale, quail, cuckoo.
listen_for.timing: II, Scene by the Brook, at the closing cadenza
listen_for.detail: Wikipedia: Beethoven labels 'the nightingale (flute), quail (oboe), and cuckoo (two clarinets)' in the score itself.

listen_for.hook: Disney put it in Fantasia, and gave it centaurs.
listen_for.detail: Wikipedia notes its appearance in Disney's Fantasia (1940), which introduced the work to a mass audience.

conflicts.resolution: 1808 recorded; the earlier sketch material noted in place.note

unknowns: How far back the pastoral sketches genuinely run; Grove does not date them.

No roster of the 22 December 1808 benefit concert survives. Brown infers the Theater an der Wien's normal strength of 6 to 8 first violins and the rest in proportion, so the card counts the score's parts instead.
